title: Pentagon launches pilot program that will use AI to manage sensitive information
gist: A memo from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg orders a six-month small-scale pilot of the Air Force's AI-based Automated Classification Management Environment (ACME), which could become the DOD's single authoritative reference for original classification decisions. CNAS fellow Josh Wallin sees gains against over-classification and stovepiping but warns of faster-scale misclassification, aggregation risks, ally cyber weaknesses, and a permanent need for human oversight.

insights.claim: Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg issued a memo directing an initial small-scale deployment of an automated, AI-backed security classification capability within six months, using the Air Force-developed ACME system with the Air Force's top civilian official as executive agent.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Signals a concrete DOD procurement and deployment path for AI in core information-governance workflows, relevant to defense-AI vendors.
insights.quote: Within the next six months, the department will start an “initial small-scale deployment of an automated security classification capability”

insights.claim: If the Pentagon's AI classification pilot succeeds, the automated system is intended to become the single digital authoritative reference for all DOD original classification decisions, a role historically held by specially designated human officials.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Shifting a statutory-style human authority to software would be a major precedent for AI decision rights inside government.
insights.quote: the automated system will eventually serve as “the single, digital authoritative reference” for all of the DOD’s original classification decisions

insights.claim: The Feinberg memo argues that outdated classification and declassification procedures cause incorrect classifications, impede interoperability, slow innovation by trapping data in stovepipes, and erode public trust by delaying release of critical information.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Frames data-access modernization as a mission priority, supporting budget flows to defense data-management and AI tooling.
insights.quote: The dysfunction caused by these procedures leads to incorrect classifications that burden our national security systems, impede interoperability, and slows innovation by trapping vital data in stovepipes
insights.locator: The dysfunction caused by these procedures

insights.claim: A DOD request for information issued in August described the decades-old manual classification process as incompatible with digital-age information volume, citing hundreds of original classification authorities using archaic programs, high error rates, frequent over-classification, and a roughly 140-million-page hardcopy backlog.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A 140-million-page backlog quantifies a large addressable digitization and AI-classification workload for government contractors.
insights.quote: The notification said the DOD has a roughly 140-million-page hardcopy backlog.
insights.locator: The notice said there are hundreds

insights.claim: The Pentagon did not disclose which underlying AI models would power its classification pilot or whether it had concerns about using AI to manage sensitive information.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Model vendor selection for classified workloads remains an open question and a potential contract catalyst.
insights.locator: The Pentagon did not immediately answer

insights.claim: The Pentagon's AI classification push comes amid public concern after several high-profile incidents in recent months where AI evaded human oversight, while defense officials argue AI is too powerful to sideline given adversaries also use it.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Defense AI adoption is proceeding despite a regulatory backlash, implying a divergence between civilian AI regulation and military deployment.
insights.locator: Feinberg’s directive comes amid deep public concerns

insights.claim: CNAS fellow Josh Wallin argues that automating classification could reduce human misclassification (over-protection, under-protection, mislabeling) and cut information stovepiping, which matters because modern conflict shows fast information flow is an advantage over adversaries.
insights.speaker: Josh Wallin
entities: Center for a New American Security
insights.so_what: Faster intelligence sharing is framed as a warfighting edge, strengthening the case for defense data/AI spending.

insights.claim: Josh Wallin says over-classified information can be stalled by delayed reviews and withheld from organizations that need it, including coalition partners for whom information sharing is critical to coordination.
insights.speaker: Josh Wallin
insights.so_what: Coalition interoperability is a driver for allied data-sharing infrastructure investment.
insights.quote: in a coalition environment where information sharing is critical to coordination.

insights.claim: Josh Wallin contends that the vast majority of government information is not so sensitive that misclassification is a serious worry, validating the memo's concerns about over-classification.
insights.speaker: Josh Wallin
insights.so_what: Suggests much classified material could be safely declassified or shared, expanding usable defense data for AI and analytics.
insights.quote: I think that you would actually find that in a lot of cases, the vast majority of information isn’t necessarily so sensitive that you’re worried about a misclassification.
insights.locator: They are right when they say

insights.claim: AI-backed classification systems could produce misclassification at a faster scale, and allies or partners with weaker cybersecurity who receive information faster could become a route for adversaries to obtain U.S. data.
insights.speaker: Josh Wallin
insights.so_what: Faster sharing raises demand for allied cybersecurity hardening and could create leak-driven policy reversals.
insights.quote: Is there a potential for an adversary to get information via them, even if they can’t get it through [U.S. systems]?
insights.locator: But, there is still a risk

insights.claim: Automated declassification may accelerate an aggregate effect in which adversaries piece together sensitive information from many individually declassified fragments.
insights.speaker: Josh Wallin
insights.so_what: A second-order security risk that could slow or constrain AI-driven declassification programs.

insights.claim: Josh Wallin questioned the pilot's short timeline and argues that misclassifications are inevitable in both human and AI processes, so human oversight of AI classification will have to persist indefinitely and complete trust will never be achieved.
insights.speaker: Josh Wallin
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop requirements imply AI will augment rather than replace classification staff, tempering labor-savings expectations.
insights.quote: That’s going to have to persist forever. This situation is going to evolve over time. The system itself is going to evolve over time, so you’re never going to have complete 100% trust.
insights.locator: I would want to know procedurally
